newsitem.title: CANADA: Smokers rejoice after Toronto amends smoking ban.
newsitem.headline: Smokers rejoice after Toronto amends smoking ban.

text.p: Smoking is back by popular demand in Canada's largest city after Toronto softened one of North America's most draconian laws against public puffing.

Bar and restaurant owners, who led the fight to amend the anti-smoking law, were rejoicing on Wednesday at the return of tobacco lovers, who had been banned last month from smoking in their establishments.

Karim Jamal, owner of a donut shop in an underground mall beneath Toronto's municipal offices, said business was booming again after a 50 percent drop following the March 3 implementation of the anti-smoking measure.
"When there was no smoking, there was no one here and now you can see there is nowhere to sit," he said.
He said that during the ban, workers in the upstairs building retreated to a smoking room dubbed the "gas chamber" because of the thick wall of smoke inside.

Less than six weeks after barring smoking in bars and restaurants without separate smoking rooms, Toronto city councilors caved in earlier this week to the C$735 million (US$525 million) restaurant industry, which said the ban killed up to 30 percent of their business.
The amended law, passed at a raucous city council session late on Monday, allowed smoking in 10 percent of the open seating in bars and restaurants.
The previous measure, designed to protect people against the dangers of second-hand smoke, had been widely criticised, and was flouted by many restaurant owners and patrons.

Some bar and restaurant owners said they had let smokers ignore the ban in order to keep their business. They said some customers were so outraged by the ban that they even lit up in areas reserved for non-smokers before the ban.

"If the management didn't get on top of them (smokers), customers were lighting up all over the place and there was some strife from customer to customer," said Tony Florsham, Ontario director of operations for The Elephant and Castle restaurant chain.
But Toronto's public health department vowed to continue its drive to rid Toronto's bars and public places of the noxious fumes from cigarette smoke.
The department said it would maintain its snitch line for violators of the amended bylaw and press to have the ban reinstituted as early as next year.

"Right now we feel this is a step back for health and we will continue to work toward the elimination (of smoking in restaurants and bars) by the year 2000, which is what council is committed to," health department spokeswoman Jackie Smith said.
